sections.formation:
## Formation

J.M.J formation is person oriented, contextualized and integral. Formation is a process of growing into the likeness of Christ. The primary end of formation is to initiate the Formee to God’s unique call, in the specific charism, Spirituality, Ministry and Mission of our congregation. Formation of us and the new members of our society is a continuous process of updating and adapting to the challenging situations and needs and putting on the mind of Christ. In other words, the final objective of Consecrated life is not just any ideal of perfection, nor is it a specific operational availability of the individual or the group, but it is the formation in the heart of the consecrated person, to have the “sentiments of the Son”.

Formees respond to God’s call in tune with the Charism of society. The formee is initiated to discern, discover and respond to God’s unique call in the specific Charism, Spirituality ‘ministry and mission of our Congregation. This identity is necessary not only for the maturity of the members in order to live and work in conformity with the foundational Charism, but also for the identity and unity of the institute. Formation of the young is a matter of greatest importance to the Congregation. The thrust of formation must enable them to grow in freedom, so that vocational values and ideals are internalized and personalized. Thus the formees are led to a deep inner freedom of heart. Formation must facilitate personal growth and self-awareness and conscious motivation for ongoing conversion, so that they can gradually acquire a mature sense of out look to form themselves in freedom with responsibility.

## Stages of Formation

### Pre-Postulancy

The Congregation must create a climate for our young person’s where they can live together with other members of the congregation. The new members bring freshness of life and new ideas, but it has to be developed in the spirit of our charism. At the same time, the Congregation must take note of the marvels and innate goodness of each Former, to flourish and reach the highest development and growth for the good of the individual, the Society and the world at large.

The candidate (pre-postulant) must be open to the guidance given in order that she may form herself. It is necessary to introduce them to our apostolic life by way of explaining and partly involving them and witnessing the apostolic work carried out in our communities.

The specific vocation and character of our Congregation, namely ‘An Ever-Adaptable Apostolic Availability’ should appeal to them.

### Postulancy

When a person feels drawn to experience the life and ministry of the J.M.J Congregation, she makes it known to the Provincial Superior. After a proper dialogue with the Former, she is accepted to the Congregation officially by handing over the Medal of our Holy patrons, Jesus Mary and Joseph. She makes 5 days retreat prior to her entrance to Postulancy.

The period of Postulancy generally lasts for one year. The Provincial Superior, with the consent of her Council may extent the time for another six months, for good reasons.

### Novitiate

After having lived the period of Postulancy for one year, and has attained the required human and Christian maturity, the Postulant may make known her wish in writing to the Provincial Superior.

The Provincial Superior, after a proper dialogue with the Postulant and in consultation with her council, admits the postulant to the Novitiate. The postulant makes a retreat of 8 days prior to her entrance to Novitiate. Novitiate is the beginning of the life in the Congregation and is a time of intensive formation. During the Novitiate the novice tests herself, finding out whether the life chosen by her, as defined in the Constitutions, inspires her and affords her the opportunity of realizing her ideals. She must seriously try to find her place in the Congregation. Novice on her side puts herself open to our Charism and to the guidance given. Ultimately it is she herself bears the responsibility of her formation. The young novice decides to grow into a mature person, who can launch out with freedom and responsibility in the service to the kingdom.

A novice, who has the genuine vocation to the religious life, will have strong faith, love for prayer, readiness to sacrifice, call to service and a life of communication & Commitment.

The Novitiate lasts for two years

The Novitiate lasts for two years. This period covers the canonical year. The Provincial Superior with the consent of her council may, extend the time of novitiate for a good reason, but not more than 6 months. Besides the programme given during the first year, the second year is concentrated on apostolic formation and Consecration of the novice to Lord. The Lord is the foundation and ultimate aim of a novice.

### Temporary Profession

After the first profession made at the close of the noviciate, there is a period of six to nine years, before the final commitment when sisters are placed in different communities either engaged in one or the other apostolate or in furthering their professional training.

Formation is an ongoing process. This demands that spiritual knowledge be constantly kept up; thus the personal spiritual development of the sisters promotes our apostolic endeavour an indispensable requirement for all forms of apostolate in being well informed about and keeping abreast of contemporary thinking. Each sister takes up the responsibility to grow spiritually and integrate the various aspects of her life. Involved in the realities of the world today and inspired by the unique role played by our holy patrons – Jesus Mary and Joseph, in the plan of salvation, we are called to grow in living our consecrated life, day by day, with deep commitment and conviction.

The Congregation offers ample opportunities at every stage through seminars, courses, meetings, interactions etc; to learn, to be enlightened and transformed.
sections.our-founder:
## Rev. Fr. Mathias Wolff, S.J. (1779–1857)

Founder of the Society of Jesus Mary Joseph

## 1. Early Life and Vocation

Rev. Fr. Mathias Wolff, S.J., was born on 9 March 1779 in Diekirch, Luxembourg, during a period of great political and religious upheaval in Europe. From his early years, he felt a deep desire to become a Jesuit priest and dedicate his life to the greater glory of God. However, the suppression of the Society of Jesus in 1773 prevented him from immediately fulfilling this aspiration.

He was ordained a diocesan priest on 25 April 1802 and served in several parishes, dedicating himself wholeheartedly to pastoral ministry. When the Society of Jesus was restored in 1814, he pursued his long-cherished vocation and entered the Jesuit novitiate in Belgium in 1815. In 1816, he began his Jesuit mission in the Netherlands, where he would spend the greater part of his apostolic life.

## 2. His Mission in the Netherlands

Fr. Wolff arrived in the Netherlands at a time when Catholics faced considerable religious and social challenges. The Catholic community needed spiritual guidance, education, and opportunities to practise and strengthen its faith. He responded to these needs with extraordinary zeal, courage, and pastoral sensitivity.

Through preaching, catechesis, retreats, spiritual guidance, and patient ministry, he worked to renew the faith of the people. His commitment extended beyond the ordinary boundaries of pastoral service. He recognised the needs of the people around him and sought practical ways to respond, especially to those who were deprived of opportunities and support.

His life was marked by unwavering trust in Divine Providence, perseverance amid difficulties, and a deep desire to bring people closer to Christ.

## 3. The Foundation of the Society of Jesus Mary Joseph

One of Fr. Wolff’s most significant contributions was the foundation of the Society of Jesus Mary Joseph (JMJ) on 29 July 1822 at Amersfoort, in the Netherlands. Recognising the urgent need for Catholic education, particularly for girls, he envisioned a Society of women religious who would help strengthen the faith of the people through education and dedicated apostolic service.

The first members, including Maria Stichters, Sophia Miltner, and Lebuina van Elck, responded generously to this vision. Their formation and commitment laid the foundation for a Society that would gradually expand its mission and ministries.

Fr. Wolff guided the young Society through a challenging social and political climate. He encouraged the Sisters to remain deeply rooted in God, humble in service, and courageous in responding to the needs of the Church and society. He wanted their lives to bear witness to Christ through faith, charity, simplicity, and joyful dedication.

## 4. His Charism: Ever Adaptable Apostolic Availability

The charism of Ever Adaptable Apostolic Availability expresses the heart of Fr. Wolff’s vision and continues to inspire the mission of the JMJ Sisters.

For Fr. Wolff, apostolic availability meant being ready to respond generously to God’s call, the needs of the Church, and the changing circumstances of the world. He encouraged the Sisters to remain flexible, open to the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and willing to go wherever their service was needed.

This charism is not merely a willingness to accept assignments; it is an attitude of inner freedom, discernment, and wholehearted commitment to the mission of Christ. It calls every JMJ Sister to move beyond personal preferences and familiar surroundings when the greater good of God’s people requires it.

The Founder’s spirituality was centred on Jesus Christ and His mission. His vision invited the Sisters to unite deep prayer with active service, seeking the will of the Father and expressing their love for God through solidarity with people, especially those who are poor, vulnerable, neglected, and marginalised.

## 5. His Missionary Zeal and Personal Spirituality

Fr. Wolff’s life was characterised by deep faith, courageous leadership, perseverance, humility, and complete trust in Divine Providence. Despite opposition and personal difficulties, he continued to serve the people entrusted to his care.

His words, “I want to work for God like a giant and win as many souls as I can,” reveal his extraordinary apostolic enthusiasm. He was convinced that life was a gift to be spent generously for God and the salvation of souls.

His spirituality can be understood through these essential characteristics:

- Deep love for Jesus Christ: Christ was the centre of his life and the inspiration for his ministry.

- Trust in Divine Providence: He remained confident in God's goodness, even in difficult circumstances.

- Apostolic courage: He persevered in his mission despite opposition and challenges.

- Availability for service: He responded to the needs of the Church with generosity and flexibility.

- Solidarity with people: He sought to strengthen the faith and dignity of those who faced religious and social difficulties.

- Humility and simplicity: He encouraged the Sisters to live authentically, allowing their lives to reflect Christ.

- Perseverance in prayer and service: His pastoral ministry, spiritual guidance, and retreats reflected his commitment to nurturing the spiritual life of others.

## 6. His Heavenly Abode — 31 October 1857

In the final years of his life, Rev. Fr. Mathias Wolff, S.J., suffered an attack that affected his intellect, memory, and speech. At times, he did not recognise his fellow religious. Yet he continued to pray fervently. His reverence and recollection during Holy Mass were remarkable, and he remained faithful to his daily practice of kissing the floor every evening before going to sleep as an act of humility. Despite his serious illness, his strong constitution enabled him to recover for a time.

Although he could no longer celebrate Holy Mass or hear confessions, he continued working untiringly until the end, compiling a book of homilies. In its introduction, he wrote with characteristic humour and self-mockery: “I am now the oldest Jesuit in the Belgian and Dutch provinces. Therefore, I can say: a patriarch, but not a prophet.”

On 28 October 1857, he went to bed and did not rise again. On 31 October 1857, at ten o’clock in the morning, at the age of 78, he breathed his last, full of trust in God's mercy, just as he had always wished. It was a Saturday, the day on which his heavenly Mother, the Blessed Virgin Mary, is especially honoured.
sections.our-history:
## History of JMJ

## 1. From one founding vision to a worldwide mission

The history of the Society of Jesus Mary and Joseph is a story of faith, missionary courage, adaptability and renewal. Founded by Rev. Fr. Mathias Wolff, SJ, in the Netherlands in 1822, the Society grew from a small beginning into an international religious Society, responding to the changing needs of the Church and society.

At the heart of this history lies the charism entrusted to the Society: “An Ever-Adaptable Apostolic Availability.” This is more than a motto; it is a way of life that calls every JMJ Sister to remain rooted in Christ, discerning the will of God and responding generously to the needs of people, especially through education, healthcare, pastoral ministry and social service.

The growth of JMJ in different countries and the subsequent establishment of independent Society’s reflect the same founding spirit: the mission must continue to flourish wherever God calls the Sisters to serve.

## 2. The growth of JMJ in India: From one Province to Three

The Indian mission began in 1904, when seven Dutch JMJ pioneers arrived in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh. Their initial apostolic work focused on education, healthcare and catechetical service. Despite difficulties involving language, formation and limited resources, the Sisters gradually established new communities and expanded their mission to other parts of India.

A significant milestone came in 1962, when the Indian mission was raised to the status of a Province, with Sr. Ferdinando Klassen as its first Provincial Superior. In 1969, the Dutch Sisters handed over the administration to Indian leadership, and Sr. Josepha Rachamalla became the first Indian Provincial Superior. The Provincial House was transferred from Guntur to Hyderabad on 28 April 1970.

As the number of communities increased and the mission extended across several states, the need for a more effective administrative and pastoral structure became evident. The distances between communities made it difficult to provide timely leadership, accompany Sisters personally, coordinate apostolic activities and attend adequately to formation.

This situation led to a historic decision: the division of the single Indian Province into three autonomous Provinces - Bangalore Province, Guntur Province and Hyderabad Province in 1987. The three autonomous Provinces, Bangalore, Guntur and Hyderabad, officially began functioning on 1 July 1987. At the time of division, the Indian mission had 39 communities across six states: Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala.

The division was not merely an administrative rearrangement. It represented a new stage in the maturity of the Indian mission. The Indian Sisters had grown in leadership, responsibility and missionary experience, and the new structure enabled them to take greater ownership of the Society's future.

The three Provinces could now develop their own leadership teams, formation houses, pastoral priorities and apostolic plans while remaining united by the same Founder, charism, spirituality and mission.

## 3. The birth of Raipur Province: A new chapter in JMJ history

On 29 September 2009, Hyderabad Province was bifurcated into two autonomous Provinces: Hyderabad Province and Raipur Province. This historic development marked a significant milestone in the growth and expansion of the Society of Jesus Mary and Joseph in India.

The bifurcation was undertaken to facilitate more effective administration, strengthen the accompaniment of the Sisters and respond more closely to the needs of the communities and apostolates spread across a vast geographical area. It opened a new chapter in the history of JMJ, creating greater opportunities for missionary outreach and the development of the Society.

The purpose was not to separate the Sisters from their common heritage, but to enable the mission to grow with greater vitality and effectiveness. Rooted in the same charism and spirituality of the Founder, Fr. Mathias Wolff, SJ, both Provinces continued to share the spirit of “An Ever-Adaptable Apostolic Availability.”

## The Bifurcation of the Society in 2016

The question of restructuring the Society of Jesus Mary Joseph became an important matter of discernment at the General Chapter of 2011. After prolonged discussions and careful reflection on the prevailing circumstances of the Society, the members recognized the need to establish two independent religious institutes. The aim was to safeguard the spiritual heritage of the Founder, strengthen leadership and enable the mission to continue fruitfully in the changing circumstances of the Church and the world.

The decision emerged from the different realities experienced by the two major groups within the Society. The Provinces of the Netherlands and Indonesia had their own historical and missionary circumstances, while the Provinces of India and the Region of Ghana were experiencing growth and developing new apostolic possibilities. These developments called for structures that could respond more effectively to their respective needs.

Between 2011 and 2016, a process of dialogue and consultation took place among the General Leadership and the members of the Society, with the assistance of the Holy See. After this period of discernment, the Holy See issued a Decree on 10 September 2016, authorizing the division of the Society into two distinct religious institutes.

The two new Congregations were constituted as follows:

### 1. Congregation of the Sisters of Jesus Mary Joseph (SJMJ)

Netherlands and Indonesia: This Congregation continued the JMJ heritage through the communities and missions of the Netherlands and Indonesia. Its Generalate was subsequently established in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, following the first Congregational Chapter in 2018. The Holy See approved its first General Leadership and Constitutions on 2 February 2019.

### 2. Congregation of Jesus Mary Joseph (CJMJ)

India and Ghana: This Congregation brought together the Indian Provinces—Bangalore, Guntur, Hyderabad and Raipur—and the Region of Ghana. The first Congregational Chapter was held in May 2018, during which the first General Leadership was elected and the name of the new Congregation was determined. On 2 February 2019, the Holy See formally recognized it as a religious institute of pontifical right and approved its Constitutions ad experiment.

## Education

The seven Dutch Missionary Pioneer Sisters arrived in India on 24th Feb 1904 in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh. The beginnings of the society of JMJ Education edifice dates back to June 1904. With a few children from the villages, the sisters started a small Lower Elementary School. The sisters started keeping children with them. This was the beginning of the boarding schools in the society of JMJ, India. Gradually sisters won the confidence of the people and more girls started coming to our schools and boarding’s from villages. There was a slow and steady growth in the strength of the school.

Rev. Sr. Stanislas Swamikannu Pillai: Sr. Stanislaus is the first Indian member to join the Society of JMJ. She is the founder, the mastermind and backbone of JMJ Education apostolate in India. With her a new chapter, a new era, ushered in the Apostolate of Education in the Society of JMJ, A.P., India. A tiny Elementary School started by the pioneers was raised eventually to a full pledged High School, University Education and College of Education for Women in Andhra Pradesh.

The Education Ministries of the Congregation of Jesus Mary Joseph (JMJ), Hyderabad Province, include schools, colleges, teacher-training institutions, vocational education, and special education services. The Congregation’s educational mission is to form the human person to the fullness of life, with particular concern for the poor and marginalized.

sections.social-work:
## JMJ Social Service Society (JMJ SSS)

Promoting human dignity, empowering communities, and building a more just and inclusive society.

### About JMJ Social Service Society

JMJ Social Service Society (JMJ SSS) is the social apostolate of the Congregation of Jesus Mary Joseph (JMJ), Hyderabad Province. Inspired by the Gospel values of compassion, justice, peace, and respect for human dignity, the Society is committed to the empowerment and integral development of marginalized and disadvantaged communities, particularly women, children, youth, and other socially excluded groups.

Through various initiatives in education, healthcare, women’s empowerment, livelihood promotion, environmental protection, and community development, JMJ SSS strives to create opportunities for sustainable development and social transformation. Its presence across several districts of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh enables it to respond to local needs in collaboration with grassroots organizations, community leaders, and development partners.

Rooted in the charism of “Ever Adaptable Apostolic Availability,” entrusted to the Congregation by its Founder, Rev. Fr. Mathias Wolff, S.J., JMJ SSS seeks to respond creatively and compassionately to the changing needs of society, with particular concern for the poor, vulnerable, and marginalized.

[JMJ Social Service Society](https://jmjssshyd.org/)
sections.province-introduction:
## Who We Are

We, the Sisters of the Congregation of Jesus Mary Joseph (JMJ), Hyderabad Province, are called by the Spirit to cross the frontiers of culture, language, and belief. Through our life and mission in international communities, we strive to carry forward the mission of Christ through our apostolic ministries. Inspired by the vision and spirituality of our Founder, Rev. Fr. Mathias Wolff, S.J., we remain faithful to our religious vocation and committed to living our charism of “Ever Adaptable Apostolic Availability” in response to the evolving needs of the Church and the world.
